Core Mandate: Primary parliamentary instruments to enforce executive accountability and exercise control over the Council of Ministers.
Question Hour: First hour of every parliamentary sitting dedicated to asking and answering questions.
Timings: Lok Sabha: 11:00 AM – 12:00 Noon; Rajya Sabha: 12:00 Noon – 1:00 PM (shifted after 2014)
Parliamentary Accountability Triangle: Question Hour + Supplementary Questions + Adjournment Motions directly ensure cabinet responsibility to the legislature.
Starred Question: Requires an Oral Answer on the floor of the House; Supplementary questions are ALLOWED; Maximum limit: 20 questions listed for oral answer per day.
Unstarred Question: Requires a Written Answer laid on the table; Supplementary questions are NOT allowed.
Short Notice Question: Relates to a matter of urgent public importance; Asked with shorter notice than the standard prescribed period; Receives an oral answer; supplementary questions are ALLOWED.

Parliamentary Committees act as a primary mechanism of parliamentary control over administration, handling detailed and complex legislative scrutiny.
2 Broad Types: Standing Committees: Permanent and continuous; reconstituted annually or periodically (e.g., Financial Committees, DRSCs).
2 Broad Types: Ad-hoc Committees: Temporary; constituted for a specific inquiry/task and cease to exist after submitting their report (e.g., Joint Parliamentary Committees, Inquiry Committees).
Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs): Total 24 DRSCs: 16 under Lok Sabha + 8 under Rajya Sabha (Standard Joint ratio approx 2 : 1).

Committee on Petitions: Examines petitions and representations submitted to the House (Lok Sabha: 15 members; Rajya Sabha: 10 members; Ministers barred).

Ethics Committee (Lok Sabha): First constituted as Ad-hoc on 16 May 2000; made permanent in 2015; oversees moral/ethical member conduct; cannot take up sub-judice matters.
Consultative Committees: Constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (not parliamentary committees per se); MPs from specific zones/ministries are members.

Election Machinery: Election Commission of India (Art. 324): Conducts elections for President, Vice-President, Parliament (LS & RS), and State Legislatures (Assemblies & Councils).
Election Machinery: State Election Commission (Arts. 243K & 243ZA): Conducts elections for Panchayats and Municipalities.

Presiding Officers: Chosen/elected internally by respective Houses (Art. 93 for Lok Sabha Speaker/Deputy Speaker; Art. 178 for Assembly; Art. 89(2) for RS Deputy Chairman; Art. 182 for Council Chairman)—NOT conducted by ECI.
Notification Trap: Election notifications are issued by the President (Parliament) or Governor (State Legislature); ECI recommends dates and administers the schedule.
Dispute Adjudication: Handled exclusively by the Judiciary via election petitions (Presidential/Vice-Presidential disputes handled exclusively by the Supreme Court under Art. 71)—NOT by ECI.
Right to Vote & Be Elected: Treated as a Legal/Statutory Right (not a Fundamental Right); voting age lowered from 21 to 18 via the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 (effective 1989).

t: President vs Vice-President: President = Elected MPs + Elected MLAs (Legislative Councils excluded); Vice-President = ALL MPs (Elected + Nominated) (State Legislatures completely excluded).
FPTP Rule: Winning candidate requires only the highest vote count among contestants, not an absolute majority (50% + 1).
Vacancy in Electoral College: A Presidential election cannot be challenged or delayed on the grounds that vacancies exist in the electoral college (Art. 71(4)).
Vote Value: MLA vote value varies from State to State based on population ratios; MP vote value is uniform across all MPs.
Core Principle: Exercise in democratic decentralisation, community participation, and local accountability (NOT central control or mere administration).
Constitutional Directive: Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organize Village Panchayats as units of self-government.
Historical Landmarks: Charles Metcalfe: Described Indian village communities as "Little Republics".
Historical Landmarks: Lord Ripon (1882 Resolution): Recognized as the Father of Local Self-Government in India.
Historical Landmarks: GoI Act, 1919: Local Self-Government made a Transferred Subject under provincial dyarchy.
Historical Landmarks: First Panchayati Raj State: Rajasthan (Nagaur District on 2 October 1959), followed second by Andhra Pradesh.
Historical Landmarks: First Municipal Corporation: Madras (1688).
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): Recommended 3-tier Panchayati Raj (Gram Panchayat -- Panchayat Samiti -- Zila Parishad); recognized as the Architect of Panchayati Raj.
Ashok Mehta Committee (1977–78): Recommended a 2-tier model and separate Nyaya Panchayats.
Hanumantha Rao Committee (1983): Decentralisation of powers/finance and district planning bodies.
G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): Revitalization and representative character of Panchayats.
L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): Recommended constitutional status and greater financial resources for local bodies.

t: Art. 243A (Gram Sabha): Village-level general assembly of all persons registered in the village electoral rolls.
Art. 243B (Three-Tier System & Exemption): Mandatory 3-tier structure; Intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional for States with a population ≤20 Lakhs.
Art. 243C & 243R (Composition & Age): State Legislature regulates composition; minimum qualifying age is 21 years (for both Panchayats and Municipalities).
Art. 243D & 243T (Reservations): Mandatory reservation of not less than 1/3rd (≥33%) of total seats and chairpersons for women.
Art. 243E & 243U (Tenure & Dissolution): Fixed term of 5 years; if dissolved prematurely, elections must be held within 6 months (not required if remaining term is < 6 months).
Art. 243G & 243W (Powers & Responsibilities): Powers over economic development, social justice, sanitation, public health, local utilities, and roads/bridges.
Art. 243-I & 243-Y (State Finance Commission): Constituted every 5 years by the Governor to review local finance distribution.
Art. 243J & 243Z (Accounts & Audit): State Legislature provides for maintenance and audit of accounts.
Art. 243K & 243ZA (State Election Commission): Superintendence, direction, and conduct of local elections.

Functional Domain Trap: Local Self-Government includes public health, sanitation, water supply, and rural development; Maintenance of Public Order and Judicial Review are NOT local-government functions.
Gram Sabha vs Gram Panchayat: Gram Sabha is the entire electorate (body of registered voters); Gram Panchayat is the elected executive body.
Audit Authority Trap: Panchayat audit laws are enacted by the State Legislature (NOT the Union Parliament, CAG, or District Collector).
Intermediate Level Exemption: Populated threshold where intermediate tier is optional is 20 Lakhs.
Summoning: The President calls each House of Parliament to meet under Article 85; the maximum gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months.
Session: The period between the first sitting of a House and its prorogation or dissolution (Standard sessions: Budget, Monsoon, Winter).
Sitting: A daily meeting of the House during a session (comprises morning and post-lunch sittings).
Adjournment: Terminates a daily sitting for a specified time (hours, days, or weeks); exercised by the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman).
Adjournment Sine Die: Terminating a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly.
Prorogation: Terminates a session of the House (not the House itself); issued by the President under Article 85(2).
Dissolution: Ends the life of the House entirely; applies only to Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha is a permanent House).
Recess: The period between the prorogation of a session and the commencement of a new session (e.g., when Parliament is in recess, the President may issue ordinances under Art. 123).
Quorum: The minimum number of members required to be present to conduct official business (1/10th of total membership of the House under Art. 100).
Question Hour: The first hour of every sitting dedicated to asking and answering questions.
Zero Hour: An Indian parliamentary innovation (since early 1960s) following Question Hour to raise urgent public matters without prior formal notice.
Closure Motion: A motion moved to cut short debate and put the matter directly to vote.
Guillotine: A specific form of closure where, upon the expiry of allotted time, all undiscussed clauses or demands for grants are put to vote immediately.

t: Annual Financial Statement: Constitutional nomenclature for the Union Budget under Article 112.
Appropriation Bill (Art. 114): Statutory authorization enabling withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India for voted grants and charged expenditure.
Vote on Account (Art. 116): Advance grant given by Lok Sabha to cover estimated expenditure for a part of the financial year pending budget passage.
Vote of Credit: An unexpected, blank-check financial grant for an emergency or indefinite demand whose details cannot be stated in a budget.
Charged Expenditure: Non-votable expenditure paid directly out of the Consolidated Fund of India (can only be discussed).
The Three Cut Motions: Policy Cut: Move to reduce the demand to ₹1 (expresses complete disapproval of the underlying policy).
The Three Cut Motions: Economy Cut: Move to reduce the demand by a specified amount (demands economy in expenditure).
The Three Cut Motions: Token Cut: Move to reduce the demand by ₹100 (ventilates a specific grievance within the Government's sphere of responsibility).
Habeas Corpus ("To have the body"): Quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention.
Mandamus ("We Command"): Directs a public official, inferior court, or statutory authority to perform a mandatory public/legal duty.
Prohibition ("To Forbid"): Issued by a higher court to prevent an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction (preventive).
Certiorari ("To be Certified"): Issued by a higher court to quash an order already passed by an inferior court/tribunal due to lack of jurisdiction or error of law (curative and preventive).
Quo-Warranto ("By what warrant/authority"): Inquires into the legality of a person's claim to a public office to prevent illegal usurpation.
Judicial Review: Inherent power of constitutional courts to review legislative enactments and executive actions against constitutional validity.
Basic Structure Doctrine: Propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); core structural features of the Constitution that cannot be abrogated or destroyed even via Article 368.
Pardon: Completely absorbs and removes both the sentence and conviction, placing the offender in the same position as if the offense had never been committed.
Commutation: Substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form (e.g., Death sentence -- Rigorous Life Imprisonment).
Remission: Reduces the period/duration of the sentence without changing its fundamental character (e.g., 2 years rigorous imprisonment -- 1 year rigorous imprisonment).
Respite: Awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty due to special personal circumstances (e.g., pregnancy, mental/physical disability).
Reprieve: Grants a temporary stay or postponement of the execution of a sentence (especially death penalty) to allow time to seek Presidential pardon.
First-Past-the-Post (FPTP): Plurality voting system where the candidate securing the highest number of valid votes is declared elected (absolute majority >50% not required).

Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote (PR-STV): Multi-preference quota-based indirect voting system used for President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha, and Legislative Councils to ensure proportional representation.
Delimitation: The statutory process of redrawing territorial constituency boundaries based on recent census figures to enforce equal representation.

Dyarchy ("Double Rule"): System introduced in provinces under the GoI Act, 1919, splitting administrative subjects into Reserved (Governor + Executive Council) and Transferred (Governor + Popular Ministers).
Collective Responsibility (Art. 75(3)): Principle that the Council of Ministers is collectively answerable to the popular House (Lok Sabha); all ministers sink or swim together.

Adjournment vs Prorogation vs Dissolution: Adjournment terminates a Sitting (Speaker/Presiding Officer); Prorogation terminates a Session (President/Governor); Dissolution terminates the House (President/Governor).
Cut Motion Amounts: Policy Cut = ₹1 | Token Cut = ₹100 | Economy Cut = Specified amount.
Right to Vote: It is a Legal/Statutory Right, not a Fundamental Right.
Local Self-Government Exemption: 3-tier Panchayati Raj applies everywhere, but the Intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti) is optional in States with a population of ≤20 Lakhs.
